Generalized geology and cross sections from the Juana Díaz, Ponce, and Hormigueros areas indicate that the surface is primarily composed of unconsolidated Quaternary alluvial and other surficial deposits, underlain by Cretaceous-Tertiary limestone and terrigenous clastic formations. In the South Coast and Southern Slopes region of Puerto Rico, approximately 10 wells were examined, including CPR hydrocarbon wells, South Coast wells, Punta Cuchara, Central Aguirre, Arroyo, Patilla, and Santa Isabel wells (Figure 6). (2002) 2.1.2 Geology and Hydrogeology, San Juan Metropolitan Area After millions of years of volcanic activity (early Cretaceous to mid-Miocene), layers of sediments, mainly carbonates, formed in the northern basin during the Oligocene. These layers later tilted northward due to more recent tectonics and thinned toward the east, where the San Juan structural arch limited thickness to less than 100 m. In the San Juan Metropolitan Area (SJMA), sedimentary units are thinner, more variable, and more heavily influenced by structural and depositional transitions compared to the broader North Coast basin. The area is predominantly covered by Quaternary surficial deposits, with limited exposures of tertiary formations such as the Aymamón and Aguada limestones, which are more intact further south near Guaynabo and Bayamón (Kaye 1959). The aquifer system in the SJMA is distinct due to its geologic complexity, along with anthropogenic factors like urbanization and historical groundwater use. The upper aquifer is often poorly developed due to erosion and karstification and is typically brackish or saline (Anderson 1976). The middle confining unit, consisting of clay-rich facies of the Cibao Formation, is locally leaky, allowing some vertical water movement (Renken et al. 2002). The lower aquifer, primarily composed of the Mucarabones Sand and lower Cibao Formation, offers variable but generally modest yields of groundwater. Salinity increases eastward beyond Río Piedras, and recharge occurs mostly near outcrop zones. The aquifer’s productivity is influenced by both lithological and structural heterogeneity (Anderson 1976; Renken et al. 2002). Much of the land surface of the SJMA is covered by younger deposits, whereas older limestone formations appear more consistently farther south, near towns such as Guaynabo and Bayamón.
